props.title: The Wicker Man

sections.content: The Wicker Man (1973) revolutionized folk horror by weaving pagan rituals with psychological dread. Sergeant Howie's investigation on Summerisle creates an escalating clash between Christian morality and ancient Celtic practices. The film's genius lies in how director Robin Hardy and writer Anthony Shaffer gradually reveal the island's true nature through seemingly innocent folk songs and traditions. This approach influenced later folk horror like Kill List (2011) and Midsommar (2019), establishing the subgenre's focus on isolated communities with sinister belief systems.

sections.content: The film's musical elements set it apart from contemporary horror. Composer Paul Giovanni's folk songs aren't mere decoration - they're narrative tools revealing the islanders' beliefs and foreshadowing Howie's fate. This innovative use of diegetic music influenced films like A Field in England (2013) and The Ritual (2017), where folk traditions become instruments of terror.

Christopher Lee's Lord Summerisle represents a departure from his Hammer Horror roles, creating a sophisticated antagonist whose educated refinement makes the island's practices more unsettling. This characterization influenced later folk horror villains, particularly in Children of the Corn (1984) and Apostle (2018), where charismatic leaders mask barbaric intentions. sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond horror into broader explorations of belief and tradition. The Village (2004) and The Other Lamb (2019) echo its themes of isolated communities and corrupted faith. The Wicker Man's ending - shocking for its era - established folk horror's tradition of unflinching conclusions, seen in modern works like The Witch (2015) and Men (2022).
